title: RaPD: Resolution-Agnostic Pixel Diffusion via Semantics-Enriched Implicit Representations

paper.title: RaPD: Resolution-Agnostic Pixel Diffusion via Semantics-Enriched Implicit Representations
paper.abstract: Abstract Natural images are continuous, yet most generative models synthesize them on discrete grids, limiting resolution-flexible generation. Continuous neural fields enable resolution-free rendering, but prior methods introduce continuity only at the decoding stage as an interpolation module, leaving the generative latent space discretized and reconstruction-oriented. We propose RaPD ( R esolution- a gnostic P ixel D iffusion), which performs diffusion in a continuous Neural Image Field (NIF) latent space. RaPD bridges this reconstruction–generation gap with Semantic Representation Guidance for generation-aware latent learning and a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer for coordinate-conditioned, scale-aware rendering. A single denoised latent can be rendered at arbitrary resolutions by changing only the query coordinates, keeping diffusion cost fixed. Experiments demonstrate superior generation quality and resolution scalability.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: RaPD supports arbitrary-resolution text-to-image generation and outperforms strong latent- and pixel-diffusion baselines [ 18 , 40 , 52 , 51 , 67 , 10 ] . The visual world is inherently continuous, yet modern image generative models mostly operate on spatially discretized representations. Whether in VAE latent or pixel space [ 57 , 18 , 40 , 27 , 55 ] , their architectures and computation are tied to discrete grids, making higher resolutions require more tokens and compute [ 82 ] . As a result, native generation at arbitrary, unseen resolutions remains challenging. In this work, we ask whether image generation can instead be formulated over “continuous pixels”, rather than discrete pixels or compressed VAE proxies. Existing arbitrary-resolution generation models typically introduce continuity only at the rendering stage. GAN models use coordinate-queried MLPs but suffer from limited generation capacity [ 1 , 63 , 4 ] . Latent diffusion-based models use flexible decoders [ 49 , 71 , 38 , 12 , 24 , 70 ] , yet diffusion itself remains in a discrete space, which ties semantics to a discrete contents and inheriting the VAE bottleneck [ 39 , 8 , 76 , 42 , 77 , 73 ] . Pixel diffusion removes the VAE [ 10 , 78 , 13 , 51 , 43 , 52 , 14 , 41 ] , but still generates on discrete grids. Even PixNerd [ 67 ] , the closest attempt, uses a patch-wise neural field mainly as an interpolation module over fixed-resolution features, rather than learning a latent that models continuous image signals for generation. This motivates a more fundamental question: can we directly generate continuous image signals? A straightforward solution is to diffuse existing continuous image representations. As shown in Fig. 2 , however, this yields poor results. The bottleneck lies in the representation itself: methods such as LIIF [ 11 ] and CLIF [ 12 ] are built for interpolation, with reconstruction training that favors local appearance cues and lightweight decoders with limited semantic aggregation. Thus, continuous representations must be made generation-aware to support high-quality arbitrary-resolution synthesis. To address this gap, we propose RaPD , a framework for directly generating continuous image signals. RaPD performs pixel-space diffusion in a continuous Neural Image Field (NIF) latent space, rather than treating neural fields merely as decoding-time interpolation modules. Since existing continuous image representations are reconstruction-oriented, RaPD first reshapes the NIF latent into a generation-aware representation through Semantic Representation Guidance (SRG), which injects semantic structure from a vision foundation model and adapts the timestep schedule to high-density continuous latents. To decode such semantically enriched latents, RaPD further introduces a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer (CQAR), which replaces local implicit decoders with coordinate-conditioned, scale-aware attention for inter-pixel semantic reasoning. At inference, a single denoised NIF latent can be rendered at arbitrary target resolutions by varying only the query coordinate grid, while the diffusion cost remains independent of output size (shown in Fig. 1 ). Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We propose RaPD, a resolution-agnostic pixel diffusion framework that directly generates continuous image signals in an NIF latent space. 2. We introduce Semantic Representation Guidance to transform reconstruction-oriented continuous latents into generation-aware representations. 3. We design a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer for spatially coherent arbitrary-resolution rendering with fixed diffusion cost.

sections.heading: Flow Matching.
sections.text: Flow matching [ 47 , 18 ] is a widely used training paradigm for diffusion models [ 64 , 27 , 66 ] . It learns a velocity field that transports Gaussian noise to the data distribution. To avoid overloading image notation, we denote a generic flow state by 𝒖 t \bm{u}_{t} . For a data sample 𝒖 1 \bm{u}_{1} , a common linear interpolation path is 𝒖 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ ϵ + t ​ 𝒖 1 , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) , \bm{u}_{t}=(1-t)\bm{\epsilon}+t\bm{u}_{1},\quad\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}), (1) where t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] . Under this convention, 𝒖 t \bm{u}_{t} evolves from Gaussian noise at t = 0 t=0 to data at t = 1 t=1 , and the target velocity is 𝒗 ⋆ = 𝒖 1 − ϵ \bm{v}^{\star}=\bm{u}_{1}-\bm{\epsilon} . For image generation, 𝒖 1 \bm{u}_{1} is typically instantiated as a spatially discretized representation, such as VAE latents [ 57 , 56 ] or image patch tokens [ 10 , 78 , 13 , 43 , 52 , 14 , 41 ] . Despite their strong performance, these representations tie the learned velocity field to finite spatial grids and token lengths, which can limit generalization to unseen resolutions [ 3 , 25 , 17 ] .

sections.heading: Neural Image Fields.
sections.text: We use 𝒙 \bm{x} to denote an RGB image and 𝒛 \bm{z} to denote its latent feature representation. Beyond discrete image grids, an image can be represented as a continuous coordinate-based function, commonly referred to as a Neural Image Field (NIF) [ 62 , 53 ] . Representative methods such as LIIF [ 11 ] and CLIF [ 12 ] parameterize an image by a feature map 𝒛 ∈ ℝ C × H × W \bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} , and render RGB values by querying continuous coordinates: 𝒙 ^ ​ ( 𝒒 ) = f ψ ​ ( 𝒛 , 𝒒 , Δ ​ 𝒄 ) , \hat{\bm{x}}(\bm{q})=f_{\psi}\big(\bm{z};\bm{q},\Delta\bm{c}\big), (2) where 𝒒 ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] 2 \bm{q}\in[-1,1]^{2} is a target coordinate, Δ ​ 𝒄 \Delta\bm{c} is the cell-size descriptor associated with the target pixel, and f ψ f_{\psi} denotes a coordinate renderer that queries features from 𝒛 \bm{z} and predicts the RGB value at 𝒒 \bm{q} . By evaluating Eq. ( 2 ) over different coordinate grids, the same representation can be rendered at arbitrary resolutions. Existing NIFs are typically trained for interpolation or reconstruction. Given a target RGB image 𝒙 tar \bm{x}_{\mathrm{tar}} defined on a coordinate grid 𝒬 tar \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tar}} , the renderer produces 𝒙 ^ tar = { f ψ ​ ( 𝒛 , 𝒒 , Δ ​ 𝒄 ​ ( 𝒒 ) ) ∣ 𝒒 ∈ 𝒬 tar } \hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{tar}}=\{f_{\psi}(\bm{z};\bm{q},\Delta\bm{c}(\bm{q}))\mid\bm{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tar}}\} . The reconstruction objective is ℒ rec = ‖ 𝒙 ^ tar − 𝒙 tar ‖ 1 + ω ​ ℒ LPIPS ​ ( 𝒙 ^ tar , 𝒙 tar ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\left\|\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{tar}}-\bm{x}_{\mathrm{tar}}\right\|_{1}+\omega\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}\big(\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{tar}},\bm{x}_{\mathrm{tar}}\big), (3) where ω \omega is the LPIPS loss weight. This reconstruction-oriented objective makes NIFs effective interpolators, but their latents are not directly generation-ready.

sections.heading: 3 Resolution-Agnostic Pixel Diffusion
sections.text: Figure 2: Reconstruction–generation gap of existing NIF representations: strong super-resolution reconstruction (top) but weak text-to-image generation (bottom). We present RaPD , a framework for text-to-image generation over continuous NIF latents. Instead of generating a discrete image grid or a fixed-resolution VAE latent, RaPD learns a generation-aware continuous NIF latent and denoises it with flow matching. The denoised latent is then rendered at arbitrary target resolutions by querying a coordinate-conditioned renderer, keeping the diffusion cost independent of output size. A straightforward baseline is to apply a PixelGen-style DiT denoiser [ 55 , 52 ] to existing NIF latents, such as LIIF [ 11 ] and CLIF [ 12 ] . As shown in Fig. 2 , these latents reconstruct well but generate poorly, exposing a reconstruction–generation gap . RaPD addresses this gap with two components: Semantic Representation Guidance (SRG), which makes NIF latents generation-aware, and Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer (CQAR), which renders queried coordinates with inter-pixel semantic reasoning.

sections.heading: 3.1 Basic Framework
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 3 , RaPD adopts a two-stage design. Stage-1 learns a generation-aware NIF latent. Given an encoder input image 𝒙 in \bm{x}_{\mathrm{in}} , an encoder E ϕ E_{\phi} maps it to a dense latent 𝒛 = E ϕ ​ ( 𝒙 in ) ∈ ℝ C × H × W \bm{z}=E_{\phi}(\bm{x}_{\mathrm{in}})\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} without spatial downsampling. Given a target coordinate 𝒒 \bm{q} , CQAR renders the corresponding RGB value as 𝒙 ^ ​ ( 𝒒 ) = f ψ CQAR ​ ( 𝒛 , 𝒒 , Δ ​ 𝒄 ) , \hat{\bm{x}}(\bm{q})=f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{CQAR}}\big(\bm{z};\bm{q},\Delta\bm{c}\big), (4) where f ψ CQAR f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{CQAR}} queries local features from 𝒛 \bm{z} at coordinate 𝒒 \bm{q} , and Δ ​ 𝒄 \Delta\bm{c} is the cell-size used by CQAR. An image at resolution H ′ × W ′ H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime} is rendered by evaluating Eq. ( 4 ) over all target coordinates. Unlike conventional NIFs trained mainly for interpolation, RaPD trains E ϕ E_{\phi} and f ψ CQAR f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{CQAR}} with SRG so that 𝒛 \bm{z} preserves coordinate-rendering capability while acquiring semantic structure useful for generation. We instantiate E ϕ E_{\phi} with an EDSR-style encoder [ 46 , 11 ] without spatial downsampling, producing a dense latent at the encoder-input resolution. In Stage-2, E ϕ E_{\phi} and f ψ CQAR f_{\psi}^{\mathrm{CQAR}} are frozen. We compute per-channel statistics 𝝁 z \bm{\mu}_{z} and 𝝈 z \bm{\sigma}_{z} over the training set and train a DiT-style denoiser D θ D_{\theta} , following the PixGen design [ 52 ] , over normalized NIF latents 𝒛 ~ = ( 𝒛 − 𝝁 z ) / 𝝈 z \tilde{\bm{z}}=(\bm{z}-\bm{\mu}_{z})/\bm{\sigma}_{z} . The denoiser is conditioned on frozen Qwen3-1.7B [ 74 ] text embeddings 𝒚 cond ∈ ℝ 128 × 2048 \bm{y}_{\mathrm{cond}}\in\mathbb{R}^{128\times 2048} and trained to predict the flow-matching velocity. At inference, integrating the learned velocity field produces a generated normalized latent 𝒛 ~ gen \tilde{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{gen}} , which is denormalized and rendered by CQAR at any requested resolution. sections.heading: 3.2 Semantic Representation Guidance
sections.text: Existing NIF latents are optimized for interpolation and reconstruction, making them poorly suited for generative modeling. We propose Semantic Representation Guidance (SRG), a unified strategy that makes NIF latents generation-aware at both the representation and diffusion-training levels. SRG consists of two components: Semantic Distillation , which injects foundation-model semantics into the dense NIF latent during Stage-1, and Latent-Density-Aware Timestep Shift , which adapts Stage-2 flow matching to the high-density SRG-shaped latent.

sections.heading: Semantic Distillation.
sections.text: How can a NIF latent be made generation-aware while retaining its ability to render continuous coordinates? We argue that the latent should not be learned from pixel reconstruction alone, but should also inherit semantic structure from a vision foundation model. We adopt a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 [ 54 ] as the semantic teacher, producing patch features 𝒕 ∈ ℝ 768 × H p × W p \bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{768\times H_{p}\times W_{p}} . Since the NIF latent 𝒛 \bm{z} has no spatial downsampling and a different channel dimension, we pool 𝒛 \bm{z} to the DINOv2 patch grid and project it with 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution, yielding student features 𝒛 proj ∈ ℝ 768 × H p × W p \bm{z}_{\mathrm{proj}}\in\mathbb{R}^{768\times H_{p}\times W_{p}} . This projection branch is used only for distillation; the original NIF latent keeps its spatial layout and channel dimension for coordinate-based rendering. The alignment loss comprises two terms that capture both local semantic content and global relational structure [ 77 , 76 , 73 ] . First, a cosine loss enforces per-position semantic agreement up to a margin: ℒ mcos = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − m cos − cos ⁡ ( 𝒛 proj ( i ) , 𝒕 ( i ) ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mcos}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\max\bigl(0,\,1-m_{\mathrm{cos}}-\cos(\bm{z}_{\mathrm{proj}}^{(i)},\bm{t}^{(i)})\bigr), (5) where N = H p × W p N=H_{p}\times W_{p} . Second, a distance-matrix similarity loss preserves the teacher’s pairwise relational geometry: ℒ mdms = 1 K 2 ​ ∑ i , j max ⁡ ( 0 , | 𝑫 z ​ [ i , j ] − 𝑫 t ​ [ i , j ] | − m dist ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mdms}}=\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\max\bigl(0,\,|\bm{D}_{z}[i,j]-\bm{D}_{t}[i,j]|-m_{\mathrm{dist}}\bigr), (6) where 𝑫 z \bm{D}_{z} and 𝑫 t \bm{D}_{t} are cosine-similarity matrices computed over K K sampled spatial positions from 𝒛 proj \bm{z}_{\mathrm{proj}} and 𝒕 \bm{t} , respectively. The final semantic distillation loss is ℒ distill = ℒ mcos + ℒ mdms \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{distill}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mcos}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mdms}} . We use m cos = 0.5 m_{\mathrm{cos}}=0.5 , m dist = 0.25 m_{\mathrm{dist}}=0.25 , and K = 256 K=256 . Unlike prior vision-feature alignment applied to downsampled VAE latents or denoiser features [ 77 , 76 , 73 ] , our alignment supervises a dense NIF latent directly. The projection branch transfers semantic structure without changing the latent layout, while the margin-based losses preserve compatibility with pixel-level reconstruction. Thus, semantic alignment acts here as formative supervision for a generation-aware continuous representation, rather than an auxiliary regularizer on an existing latent.

sections.heading: Latent-Density-Aware Timestep Shift.
sections.text: Semantic Distillation shapes the NIF latent, but Stage-2 must still learn a flow over this unusually dense representation. Unlike compressed VAE latents, the NIF latent has no spatial downsampling and retains a high-resolution coordinate-rendering layout. In flow matching, the timestep shift factor s s controls the sampled timestep distribution: t 0 = sigmoid ⁡ ( ξ ) , ξ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) , t = t 0 t 0 + ( 1 − t 0 ) ⋅ s . t_{0}=\mathrm{sigmoid}(\xi),\quad\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),\qquad t=\frac{t_{0}}{t_{0}+(1-t_{0})\cdot s}. (7) A larger s s helps the model prioritize heavy noise stages (small t t ). These stages are the most critical for generating decent content. Standard VAE-latent diffusion models typically use small shift factors, with s ∈ [ 1 , 3 ] s\in[1,3] , since their latents are spatially compressed. For NIF latents, we follow the resolution-dependent shift principle [ 18 ] and adopt a larger shift to compensate for the increased information density of the latent. As analyzed in Sec. 4.2 , both insufficient and excessive shifts degrade generation quality; we empirically set s = 32 s=32 in RaPD. Together, Semantic Distillation and Latent-Density-Aware Timestep Shift form SRG: the former shapes the latent into a semantic representation, while the latter adapts diffusion training to recover this representation during generation. sections.heading: 3.3 Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer
sections.text: While SRG provides the NIF latent with semantic structure, the renderer must exploit this structure during coordinate-based decoding. Existing implicit decoders such as LIIF [ 11 ] and CLIF [ 12 ] predict pixels from local latent features using pointwise MLPs or shallow CNNs. These local operators are effective for interpolation, but cannot reason across queried pixels and therefore underuse the semantic features injected by SRG. We address this limitation with the Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer (CQAR), shown in Fig. 4 . The key distinction of CQAR is that attention is performed over queried output-coordinate tokens, rather than over the input latent grid. For a target resolution H ′ × W ′ H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime} , CQAR constructs one token per output coordinate and processes these tokens with Swin-style windowed self-attention [ 48 ] . Each token is built from the queried latent feature, absolute coordinate, relative offset, and target cell size, making the renderer coordinate-grounded and scale-aware. Windowed self-attention over these output tokens enables global inter-pixel reasoning while keeping rendering cost scalable.

sections.heading: Coordinate Token Construction.
sections.text: Given an input latent 𝒛 ∈ ℝ C × H × W \bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W} and a target coordinate 𝒒 i , j \bm{q}_{i,j} , CQAR forms an output-coordinate token by 𝒉 i , j = ϕ in ​ ( 𝒛 nn ​ ( 𝒒 i , j ) , Δ ​ 𝒒 i , j , Δ ​ 𝒄 i , j , 𝒒 i , j ) , \bm{h}_{i,j}=\phi_{\mathrm{in}}\big(\bm{z}_{\mathrm{nn}}(\bm{q}_{i,j}),\Delta\bm{q}_{i,j},\Delta\bm{c}_{i,j},\bm{q}_{i,j}\big), (8) where 𝒛 nn ​ ( 𝒒 i , j ) \bm{z}_{\mathrm{nn}}(\bm{q}_{i,j}) is the nearest-neighbor latent feature, Δ ​ 𝒒 i , j = 𝒒 i , j − 𝒒 i , j ∗ \Delta\bm{q}_{i,j}=\bm{q}_{i,j}-\bm{q}^{*}_{i,j} is the offset from the nearest latent-grid center 𝒒 i , j ∗ \bm{q}^{*}_{i,j} , Δ ​ 𝒄 i , j \Delta\bm{c}_{i,j} is the relative cell-size descriptor converted from the raw pixel extent, and 𝒒 i , j ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] 2 \bm{q}_{i,j}\in[-1,1]^{2} is the absolute coordinate. The projected tokens are processed by windowed Transformer blocks and mapped to RGB values. Thus, each token attends to neighboring output-coordinate tokens, enabling global inter-pixel reasoning that pointwise implicit decoders lack.

sections.heading: 3.4 Training and Inference
sections.text: RaPD is trained in two stages. Stage-1 (Fig. 3 (A)) learns a semantically guided NIF latent. Stage-2 (Fig. 3 (B)) freezes the NIF encoder and CQAR, then trains a text-conditioned DiT denoiser over normalized NIF latents with flow matching. During inference(Fig. 3 (C)), the denoiser generates one normalized NIF latent, and CQAR renders the latent on any target coordinate grid.

sections.heading: 3.4.2 Inference
sections.text: At inference, we initialize Gaussian noise with the normalized NIF latent shape and integrate the learned velocity field with Euler ODE sampling [ 65 ] , using classifier-free guidance [ 28 ] . This produces a generated normalized latent 𝒛 ~ gen \tilde{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{gen}} , which is denormalized as 𝒛 ^ = 𝒛 ~ gen ​ 𝝈 z + 𝝁 z \hat{\bm{z}}=\tilde{\bm{z}}_{\mathrm{gen}}\bm{\sigma}_{z}+\bm{\mu}_{z} . For a target size ( H ′ , W ′ ) (H^{\prime},W^{\prime}) , we follow the LIIF coordinate convention [ 11 ] : 𝒒 i , j = ( 2 ​ i + 1 H ′ − 1 , 2 ​ j + 1 W ′ − 1 ) , 𝒄 i , j = ( 2 H ′ , 2 W ′ ) , \bm{q}_{i,j}=\left(\frac{2i+1}{H^{\prime}}-1,\;\frac{2j+1}{W^{\prime}}-1\right),\quad\bm{c}_{i,j}=\left(\frac{2}{H^{\prime}},\;\frac{2}{W^{\prime}}\right), (11) where 𝒄 i , j \bm{c}_{i,j} is the raw pixel extent from which CQAR derives Δ ​ 𝒄 i , j \Delta\bm{c}_{i,j} . Evaluating Eq. ( 4 ) with 𝒛 ^ \hat{\bm{z}} on this grid yields 𝒙 ^ H ′ × W ′ \hat{\bm{x}}_{H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}} . Thus, only the query grid changes across resolutions; diffusion cost remains fixed, while rendering cost scales with queried tokens, as shown in Tab. 3 .

sections.heading: Dataset and Evaluation.
sections.text: Following PixelGen [ 52 ] and DeCo [ 51 ] , we use BLIP3o [ 5 ] as the primary training corpus. RaPD is pretrained on approximately 36M images and fine-tuned on 60k curated high-quality images in 512 × 512 512\times 512 for improved visual fidelity and text-image alignment. We evaluate reconstruction with rFID [ 76 ] and text-to-image generation with GenEval [ 22 ] and DPG-Bench [ 31 ] , following the PixelGen [ 52 ] protocol for fair comparison.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: RaPD is compared with representative latent- and pixel-diffusion models. Latent-diffusion models include LDM [ 57 ] , SD3 [ 18 ] , FLUX.1-dev [ 40 ] , PixArt- α \alpha [ 7 ] , and DALL-E 3 [ 2 ] . Pixel-diffusion models include PixelFlow [ 10 ] , PixNerd [ 67 ] , DeCo [ 51 ] , and PixelGen [ 52 ] .

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: In Stage 1, we learn a 16 × 256 × 256 16\times 256\times 256 NIF latent space for 10k steps on the 36M images. Semantic distillation uses the final-layer patch tokens from a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 encoder as the teacher feature 𝒕 \bm{t} . In Stage 2, the diffusion model is pretrained for 260k steps and fine-tuned for 40k steps on 8 × 8\times NVIDIA B200 GPUs, taking about 5 days in total. At inference, we use 25 25 -step Euler ODE sampling with CFG scale 4.0 4.0 . More details can be found in Appendix. sections.heading: Qualitative Comparison.
sections.text: Fig. 5 compares RaPD with recent pixel-diffusion baselines at 512 × 512 512\times 512 . Across diverse prompts, RaPD produces more coherent global structure, cleaner local details, and fewer artifacts than competing methods. It better preserves object identity, reduces failures such as broken contours, duplicated parts, and distorted fine structures, and more reliably satisfies compositional constraints involving multiple objects, attributes, and spatial relations.

sections.text: Fig. 6 shows RaPD results at 1024 2 1024^{2} , 2048 2 2048^{2} , and 4096 2 4096^{2} on GenEval and DPG-Bench examples. Although the NIF latent is learned with limited multi-resolution supervision up to 512 2 512^{2} , RaPD generalizes well to out-of-distribution higher resolutions. The high-resolution samples remain coherent and contain clear boundaries and rich local details. The DPG-Bench results further indicate strong fidelity to long and complex prompts at large output scales.

sections.heading: Ablation on Semantic Distillation.
sections.text: Fig. 7 evaluates Semantic Distillation. Without it ( w/o distill ), generation exhibits weaker object structure and less stable semantic layouts, showing that reconstruction supervision alone is insufficient for NIF-latent text-to-image generation. Replacing DINOv2 with CLIP ( distill-CLIP ) further degrades semantic quality, supporting DINOv2 as a stronger teacher for generation-aware NIF latents.

sections.heading: Exploration of Latent-Density-Aware Timestep Shift.
sections.text: Fig. 9 studies the Latent-Density-Aware Timestep Shift in learning our dense NIF latent. Small shift values lead to weak object formation and poor semantic organization, showing that schedules suited to compressed VAE latents do not transfer well to our full-resolution NIF representation. Increasing the shift substantially improves generation quality, and s = 32 s=32 provides a better trade-off between clear object layout and rich visual detail. When the shift becomes too large ( s = 48 s=48 ), the generated images become overly simplified.

sections.heading: The Effect of CQAR.
sections.text: Fig. 2 compares CQAR with LIIF- and CLIF-style renderers on image reconstruction. CQAR produces sharper reconstructions with clearer boundaries and better recovery of fine structures. Following DC-AE 1.5 [ 9 ] , Fig. 9 visualizes the learned NIF features and shows that CQAR preserves clearer spatial details in the feature maps. Fig. 7 further compares the generation results. RaPD achieves the lowest rFID and the best visual quality, indicating that CQAR effectively alleviates the reconstruction–generation gap of continuous NIF representations. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: In this paper, we presented RaPD , which performs diffusion in a continuous Neural Image Field latent and decodes it through a coordinate-queried windowed-attention renderer, achieving resolution-agnostic image generation while keeping the diffusion cost fixed regardless of the output size. Three directions naturally extend this work: (i) scaling to larger datasets and models; (ii) extending the continuous NIF latent to controllable generation and editing; and (iii) hardware-aware inference acceleration to fully realize RaPD’s efficiency potential at high resolutions.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: RaPD still has several limitations. (1) It is trained on approximately 36 million BLIP3o images, substantially fewer than the data used by commercial-scale models such as SD3 and FLUX, which limits its absolute generation quality. (2) The frozen Qwen3-1.7B text encoder is relatively compact and may constrain complex prompt understanding compared with systems paired with larger language models. (3) The current inference stack does not yet incorporate FlashAttention [ 15 ] , fused window-attention kernels for CQAR, FP8 quantization, or compiler-level fusion; therefore, the reported latency and memory should be viewed as conservative upper bounds.

sections.heading: A.1 Image Generation and Resolution Flexibility
sections.text: Image generative models have evolved from GANs [ 23 , 34 , 36 , 37 ] through denoising diffusion probabilistic models [ 64 , 27 , 65 , 66 ] to the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) paradigm [ 55 , 50 , 20 ] , which has become the dominant backbone for high-quality image synthesis. Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [ 57 , 56 , 18 , 40 ] dramatically reduce computational cost by operating in a compressed VAE latent space, but this compression introduces an information bottleneck that degrades fine-grained spatial details and fixes the output resolution [ 39 , 8 , 76 , 42 ] . Motivated by this, pixel diffusion methods [ 78 , 13 , 43 , 51 , 10 , 52 , 14 , 41 , 29 ] bypass the VAE entirely to preserve complete spatial information, with recent work demonstrating competitive quality at resolutions up to 1024 × \times 1024 in pixel space. Tab. 4 summarizes the key differences among these method categories. Achieving resolution flexibility within these frameworks remains challenging. Within the LDM paradigm, several methods pair the diffusion process with flexible decoders to support variable output resolutions [ 49 , 71 , 38 , 12 , 24 , 70 , 68 ] ; however, the diffusion process itself still operates on a fixed-resolution compressed latent, confining the model’s semantic planning to a single scale. Early GAN-based approaches replace spatial convolutions with coordinate-queried MLPs for multi-scale synthesis [ 1 , 63 , 4 ] , but suffer from training instability and degraded quality at out-of-distribution resolutions [ 26 ] . Among pixel-space methods, PixNerd [ 67 ] is closest to resolution-agnostic generation, rendering beyond the training grid via a patch-wise neural field decoder, but its backbone transformer still processes a fixed token count at the pretrained resolution, restricting flexibility to the decoding stage alone. True arbitrary-resolution generation requires the entire pipeline to operate on representations decoupled from any fixed spatial grid.

sections.heading: A.2 Implicit Neural Representations for Generation
sections.text: Implicit neural representations (INRs) [ 62 , 53 ] model signals as continuous functions mapping coordinates to values. In the 2D image domain, LIIF [ 11 ] and MetaSR [ 32 ] established the paradigm of decoding a shared feature map at arbitrary resolutions via coordinate-conditioned MLPs. Subsequent work applied this paradigm to generation: IDM [ 21 ] performs INR decoding at every denoising step but at prohibitive cost; INFD [ 12 ] applies diffusion to INR-based latents using a convolutional rendering module (CLIF); and InfGen [ 24 ] replaces the VAE decoder with a transformer-based generator for single-step extrapolation to 4K. However, all existing INR-based representations are still optimized for reconstruction, not generation, suffering from two intertwined limitations. First, their latent features, trained with pixel-level losses as listed in Eq. 3 , encode low-level texture statistics rather than the semantic structure required by a generative model. Second, their decoders (pointwise MLPs [ 11 ] or shallow CNNs [ 12 ] ) lack the receptive field to exploit semantic features for coherent synthesis. Although recent works on foundation-model alignment, such as REPA [ 77 , 73 , 42 ] and VA-VAE [ 76 ] leverage this principle to accelerate diffusion training and balance VAE capacity respectively, our reconstruction–generation gap is fundamentally different: it concerns the semantic content of the NIF latent itself, and arises even when latent capacity is unbounded. Whereas REPA aligns denoiser features and VA-VAE shapes a separate VAE post-hoc, our Semantic Distillation directly shapes the NIF latent itself during its very first training stage, making generation-aware structure available to the diffusion process from the start. RaPD addresses both limitations jointly: Semantic Representation Guidance (SRG) enriches the latent with semantic structure through a foundation-model distillation procedure, and a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer (CQAR) replaces local decoders with coordinate-conditioned, scale-aware Transformer blocks [ 48 ] for inter-pixel semantic reasoning at arbitrary resolutions.

sections.text: To enable cross-window information exchange without breaking the linear cost of windowed attention, every odd-indexed block uses Swin-style shifted-window attention [ 48 ] . Mingyu You Affiliation: College of Electronic and Information Engineering, Tongji University Abstract Natural images are continuous, yet most generative models synthesize them on discrete grids, limiting resolution-flexible generation. Continuous neural fields enable resolution-free rendering, but prior methods introduce continuity only at the decoding stage as an interpolation module, leaving the generative latent space discretized and reconstruction-oriented. We propose RaPD ( R esolution- a gnostic P ixel D iffusion), which performs diffusion in a continuous Neural Image Field (NIF) latent space. RaPD bridges this reconstruction–generation gap with Semantic Representation Guidance for generation-aware latent learning and a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer for coordinate-conditioned, scale-aware rendering. A single denoised latent can be rendered at arbitrary resolutions by changing only the query coordinates, keeping diffusion cost fixed. Experiments demonstrate superior generation quality and resolution scalability. 1 Introduction Figure 1: RaPD supports arbitrary-resolution text-to-image generation and outperforms strong latent- and pixel-diffusion baselines [ 18 , 40 , 52 , 51 , 67 , 10 ] . The visual world is inherently continuous, yet modern image generative models mostly operate on spatially discretized representations. Whether in VAE latent or pixel space [ 57 , 18 , 40 , 27 , 55 ] , their architectures and computation are tied to discrete grids, making higher resolutions require more tokens and compute [ 82 ] . As a result, native generation at arbitrary, unseen resolutions remains challenging. In this work, we ask whether image generation can instead be formulated over “continuous pixels”, rather than discrete pixels or compressed VAE proxies. Existing arbitrary-resolution generation models typically introduce continuity only at the rendering stage. GAN models use coordinate-queried MLPs but suffer from limited generation capacity [ 1 , 63 , 4 ] . Latent diffusion-based models use flexible decoders [ 49 , 71 , 38 , 12 , 24 , 70 ] , yet diffusion itself remains in a discrete space, which ties semantics to a discrete contents and inheriting the VAE bottleneck [ 39 , 8 , 76 , 42 , 77 , 73 ] . Pixel diffusion removes the VAE [ 10 , 78 , 13 , 51 , 43 , 52 , 14 , 41 ] , but still generates on discrete grids. Even PixNerd [ 67 ] , the closest attempt, uses a patch-wise neural field mainly as an interpolation module over fixed-resolution features, rather than learning a latent that models continuous image signals for generation. This motivates a more fundamental question: can we directly generate continuous image signals? A straightforward solution is to diffuse existing continuous image representations. As shown in Fig. 2 , however, this yields poor results. The bottleneck lies in the representation itself: methods such as LIIF [ 11 ] and CLIF [ 12 ] are built for interpolation, with reconstruction training that favors local appearance cues and lightweight decoders with limited semantic aggregation. Thus, continuous representations must be made generation-aware to support high-quality arbitrary-resolution synthesis. To address this gap, we propose RaPD , a framework for directly generating continuous image signals. RaPD performs pixel-space diffusion in a continuous Neural Image Field (NIF) latent space, rather than treating neural fields merely as decoding-time interpolation modules. Since existing continuous image representations are reconstruction-oriented, RaPD first reshapes the NIF latent into a generation-aware representation through Semantic Representation Guidance (SRG), which injects semantic structure from a vision foundation model and adapts the timestep schedule to high-density continuous latents. To decode such semantically enriched latents, RaPD further introduces a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer (CQAR), which replaces local implicit decoders with coordinate-conditioned, scale-aware attention for inter-pixel semantic reasoning. At inference, a single denoised NIF latent can be rendered at arbitrary target resolutions by varying only the query coordinate grid, while the diffusion cost remains independent of output size (shown in Fig. 1 ). Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We propose RaPD, a resolution-agnostic pixel diffusion framework that directly generates continuous image signals in an NIF latent space. 2. We introduce Semantic Representation Guidance to transform reconstruction-oriented continuous latents into generation-aware representations. 3. We design a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer for spatially coherent arbitrary-resolution rendering with fixed diffusion cost. 2 Preliminaries Flow Matching. Flow matching [ 47 , 18 ] is a widely used training paradigm for diffusion models [ 64 , 27 , 66 ] . It learns a velocity field that transports Gaussian noise to the data distribution. To avoid overloading image notation, we denote a generic flow state by 𝒖 t \bm{u}_{t} . We present RaPD , a framework for text-to-image generation over continuous NIF latents. Instead of generating a discrete image grid or a fixed-resolution VAE latent, RaPD learns a generation-aware continuous NIF latent and denoises it with flow matching. The denoised latent is then rendered at arbitrary target resolutions by querying a coordinate-conditioned renderer, keeping the diffusion cost independent of output size. A straightforward baseline is to apply a PixelGen-style DiT denoiser [ 55 , 52 ] to existing NIF latents, such as LIIF [ 11 ] and CLIF [ 12 ] . As shown in Fig. 2 , these latents reconstruct well but generate poorly, exposing a reconstruction–generation gap . RaPD addresses this gap with two components: Semantic Representation Guidance (SRG), which makes NIF latents generation-aware, and Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer (CQAR), which renders queried coordinates with inter-pixel semantic reasoning. 3.1 Basic Framework As shown in Fig. 3 , RaPD adopts a two-stage design. We propose Semantic Representation Guidance (SRG), a unified strategy that makes NIF latents generation-aware at both the representation and diffusion-training levels. SRG consists of two components: Semantic Distillation , which injects foundation-model semantics into the dense NIF latent during Stage-1, and Latent-Density-Aware Timestep Shift , which adapts Stage-2 flow matching to the high-density SRG-shaped latent. Semantic Distillation. How can a NIF latent be made generation-aware while retaining its ability to render continuous coordinates? We argue that the latent should not be learned from pixel reconstruction alone, but should also inherit semantic structure from a vision foundation model. We adopt a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 [ 54 ] as the semantic teacher, producing patch features 𝒕 ∈ ℝ 768 × H p × W p \bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{768\times H_{p}\times W_{p}} . Since the NIF latent 𝒛 \bm{z} has no spatial downsampling and a different channel dimension, we pool 𝒛 \bm{z} to the DINOv2 patch grid and project it with 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution, yielding student features 𝒛 proj ∈ ℝ 768 × H p × W p \bm{z}_{\mathrm{proj}}\in\mathbb{R}^{768\times H_{p}\times W_{p}} . This projection branch is used only for distillation; the original NIF latent keeps its spatial layout and channel dimension for coordinate-based rendering. The alignment loss comprises two terms that capture both local semantic content and global relational structure [ 77 , 76 , 73 ] . Unlike compressed VAE latents, the NIF latent has no spatial downsampling and retains a high-resolution coordinate-rendering layout. Existing implicit decoders such as LIIF [ 11 ] and CLIF [ 12 ] predict pixels from local latent features using pointwise MLPs or shallow CNNs. These local operators are effective for interpolation, but cannot reason across queried pixels and therefore underuse the semantic features injected by SRG. We address this limitation with the Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer (CQAR), shown in Fig. 4 . The key distinction of CQAR is that attention is performed over queried output-coordinate tokens, rather than over the input latent grid. For a target resolution H ′ × W ′ H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime} , CQAR constructs one token per output coordinate and processes these tokens with Swin-style windowed self-attention [ 48 ] . Figure 9: Latent feature visualization. 5 Conclusion and Limitations In this paper, we presented RaPD , which performs diffusion in a continuous Neural Image Field latent and decodes it through a coordinate-queried windowed-attention renderer, achieving resolution-agnostic image generation while keeping the diffusion cost fixed regardless of the output size. Three directions naturally extend this work: (i) scaling to larger datasets and models; (ii) extending the continuous NIF latent to controllable generation and editing; and (iii) hardware-aware inference acceleration to fully realize RaPD’s efficiency potential at high resolutions. Limitations. RaPD still has several limitations. (1) It is trained on approximately 36 million BLIP3o images, substantially fewer than the data used by commercial-scale models such as SD3 and FLUX, which limits its absolute generation quality. (2) The frozen Qwen3-1.7B text encoder is relatively compact and may constrain complex prompt understanding compared with systems paired with larger language models. (3) The current inference stack does not yet incorporate FlashAttention [ 15 ] , fused window-attention kernels for CQAR, FP8 quantization, or compiler-level fusion; therefore, the reported latency and memory should be viewed as conservative upper bounds.
